title: Sylvester-Gallai Theorem via Kelly's Proof

overview.historicalContext: James Joseph Sylvester posed the problem in 1893 in the Educational Times: must every finite non-collinear point set have a line through exactly two of its points? No solution appeared for nearly 50 years until Tibor Gallai (born Tibor Grünwald) proved it in 1944 using a topological argument. L.M. Kelly published his celebrated one-paragraph proof in 1948 in the American Mathematical Monthly, using a purely extremal argument that has become a staple of combinatorial geometry courses. The theorem occupies a central place in incidence geometry, with deep connections to the Hesse configuration (the unique non-realizable arrangement over $\mathbb{R}$ but realizable over $\mathbb{C}$) and to the Green-Tao theorem (2013), which establishes that $n$ non-collinear points determine at least $n/2$ ordinary lines for sufficiently large $n$. The Sylvester-Gallai theorem fails over $\mathbb{C}$: the inflection points of a smooth cubic curve provide a counterexample.
overview.problemStatement: For any finite set of $\geq 3$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one line, prove there exists a line through exactly 2 of the points.
overview.text: Formalizes Sylvester-Gallai via Kelly's elegant minimum-distance proof.
overview.proofStrategy: Kelly's proof: (1) Among all pairs (point $p$, line $\ell$ through $\geq 2$ points) with $p \notin \ell$, choose the pair minimizing $d(p, \ell)$. (2) If $\ell$ has $\geq 3$ points, coordinate geometry shows we can find a strictly closer pair. (3) Contradiction, so $\ell$ has exactly 2 points.
keyInsights: Kelly's proof is purely extremal: minimize $d(p, \ell)$ over all (point, line) pairs, then show $\ge 3$ collinear points on $\ell$ yields a strictly closer pair, contradicting minimality. No topology, no projective duality—just the well-ordering of finite sets.

The coordinate calculation is the proof's only non-trivial step: placing the foot at the origin with $\ell$ along the $x$-axis, $d(a, \overline{pc}) = h(\gamma-\alpha)/\sqrt{h^2+\gamma^2} < h$ because $\alpha(\alpha-2\gamma) \le 0$ when $0 \le \alpha \le \gamma$.

The formalization separates the geometric inequality (axiomatized as `kelly_distance_lemma`) from the combinatorial setup (the sorry in `sylvester_gallai`), cleanly identifying the two proof obligations.

The Sylvester-Gallai theorem fails over $\mathbb{C}$: the 9 inflection points of a smooth cubic curve satisfy every line through 2 of them passing through a third. This failure highlights the essential role of the real ordered field in Kelly's argument ($h^2 > 0$).

Sylvester-Gallai is the qualitative foundation for Beck's theorem (1983): either $\geq n/C$ points are collinear, or the points determine $\geq n^2/C$ distinct lines — there is no 'middle ground' in line determination

sections.title: Problem History and Imports
sections.summary: Module docstring with full historical timeline (Sylvester 1893, Gallai 1944, Kelly 1948, Green-Tao 2013), axiom status, and references. Imports SimpleGraph basics, InnerProductSpace for distance, and Finset.

sections.title: Basic Geometry: Points, Collinearity, Lemmas
sections.summary: Defines Point as ℝ × ℝ, Collinear via parametric lines (c - a = t(b - a)), and proves two lemmas: collinear_self_left (t = 0) and collinear_comm (t ↦ 1-t with degenerate case handling).
sections.mathContext: Collinearity: $c$ lies on line $\overline{ab}$ iff $\exists t \in \mathbb{R}: c = a + t(b-a)$. Equivalently, the cross product $(b-a) \times (c-a) = 0$.

sections.title: Ordinary Lines and Theorem Statement
sections.summary: Defines AllCollinear (exists a line containing all points), IsOrdinaryLine (line through exactly 2 points of S), HasOrdinaryLine (existence). These predicates cleanly separate the hypothesis and conclusion of Sylvester-Gallai.
sections.mathContext: An ordinary line of $S$ is $\ell$ with $|\ell \cap S| = 2$. The non-collinearity hypothesis $\neg\text{AllCollinear}(S)$ ensures points are in 'general position' (not all on one line).

sections.title: Kelly's Key Lemma and Point-Line Distance
sections.summary: Defines pointLineDistance via the cross product formula. Proves kelly_distance_lemma via 6-case analysis on foot parameter: in each case finds a strictly closer (point,line) pair, contradicting minimality.
sections.mathContext: After placing the foot at the origin: $d(a, \overline{pc}) = \frac{h|\gamma-\alpha|}{\sqrt{h^2+\gamma^2}} < h = d(p, \ell)$ because $\alpha(\alpha-2\gamma) \le 0$ when $0 \le \alpha \le \gamma$.

sections.title: Sylvester-Gallai Main Theorem
sections.summary: States and proves sylvester_gallai: by contradiction, assumes no ordinary line, uses Finset.exists_min_image to extract the minimum-distance pair, then applies kelly_distance_lemma for contradiction. No sorry.
sections.mathContext: The proof structure: $\neg\text{HasOrdinaryLine}(S) \Rightarrow$ every line through 2 points of $S$ has $\ge 3$ points $\Rightarrow$ Kelly's lemma applies to the minimum-distance pair $\Rightarrow \bot$.

conclusion.summary: Fully verifies the Sylvester-Gallai theorem via Kelly's 1948 extremal argument. Zero axioms, zero sorries. kelly_distance_lemma proved by 6-case coordinate geometry; sylvester_gallai proved by Finset minimum extraction.
conclusion.implications: This formalization provides a clean Lean 4 foundation for the Sylvester-Gallai theorem, one of the central results in combinatorial geometry. The modular separation of the geometric inequality from the extremal setup means the axiom can be eliminated independently (it is a candidate for Aristotle proof search). Once complete, it enables formal work toward the Green-Tao ordinary lines theorem ($\ge n/2$ ordinary lines for large $n$) and Beck's theorem on point-line incidences.
